subject: Help with Fixed and Random Factors in procD.lm

messages.author: d651d65738f1efef
messages.subject: Help with Fixed and Random Factors in procD.lm
parts:
Hi all,

I hope you're doing well.

I’m currently working with 2D shape configurations (symmetric and asymmetric) of the head, extracted using the bilat.symmetry() function, from two species of triatomines with both sexes. The populations are characterized by an anthropization gradient with three levels (low, intermediate, and high), and I’m treating these variables as my fixed factors. Additionally, I have the locality where the individuals were captured, which I’m considering as a random factor.

The model I’ve been using looks like this:

  LMC.SIM.aov.null <- procD.lm(LMC.AFA$symm.shape ~ 1, iter = 9999, RRPP = TRUE) 

LMC.SIM.aov <- procD.lm(LMC.AFA$symm.shape ~ LMC1$LID * LMC1$sexo * LMC1$especie, block = LMC1$localidad, iter = 9999, RRPP = TRUE) 

anova(LMC.SIM.aov.null, LMC.SIM.aov) summary(LMC.SIM.aov) 

 par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(LMC.SIM.aov, type = "diagnostics")

gp.SIM<- interaction(LMC1$sexo,LMC1$especie)
PR.SIM<-pairwise(LMC.SIM.aov,LMC.SIM.aov.null, groups = gp.SIM)

summary(PR.SIM, test.type = "dist", confidence = 0.95, stat.table = TRUE)

My main question is whether I’m modeling the random factor (locality) correctly. Specifically, is it appropriate to use the argument block = "localidad" in this case?

Additionally, I’d appreciate any recommendations for graphical methods to report the results of this model. I also wanted to ask if there are other model validation approaches available within procD.lm, apart from inspecting the residuals plots.

Thanks in advance for your help!

Best regards,
Federico

messages.author: fbfd20ce829c6c6c
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with Fixed and Random Factors in procD.lm
parts:
Hi Federico, 

I just wanted to add a perspective here regarding your locality data. 

If you have GPS coordinates and can estimate geographical distances among sites, it might be preferable to use the geographic distance matrix as input to the model in the form of a covariance matrix (use the Cov = argument in procD.lm) representing how you think covariation in your shapes is structured among sites. 

If you choose to use this approach, you might find cov.spatial in the geoR library useful, where you can specify if covariance between localities decays with distance following different functions (a Gaussian, exponential, etc.). 

Best,
Bryan

messages.author: fbfd20ce829c6c6c
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Help with Fixed and Random Factors in procD.lm
parts:
Your data might already show spatial dependence in a variogram and you can always plot variability among data points vs distance before generating any matrices.

In addition to the raw data variogram from above, it might also be helpful to use an AIC approach to choose among a set spatial dependence structures by creating variograms from the residuals of alternative models. This is important to take covariates into account. Included among these alternative models you can compare a model with no spatial dependence and this is preferable to only picking one matrix. For example, residuals from models with exponential decay of correlations among sites will have a different pattern than the same but with Gaussian decay of similarities among sites, but both might perform better or similar to a model without spatial dependence (this is data specific).

Cheers,
Bryan

Dear Bryan,

I hope you are doing well.

I am reaching out to seek your advice regarding an issue I encountered with my spatial analysis. First, I obtained a variogram model to represent the spatial dependency of shape data. For the variogram, I used the first PC of the symmetric shape component derived from the bilat.symm function as the response variable. I then developed the variogram for my study area, with the following model parameters:

likfit: estimated model parameters:
   beta     tausq   sigmasq       phi
"-0.3230" " 0.2374" " 0.2625" " 0.3794"
Practical Range with cor=0.05 for asymptotic range: 0.6566316

  Using the obtained values for sigmasq and phi, I calculated the covariance matrix with the function cov.spatial, as follows:

cov_matrix <- cov.spatial(dist_matrix, cov.pars = c(0.2625, 0.3794), cov.model = "gaussian")

Here, dist_matrix contains the distances in kilometers between sampling points, and the resulting covariance matrix is 288x288, corresponding to the individuals collected. The matrix returns values between 0 and 0.2625. I did not reduce the matrix size, as doing so would cause issues with the procD.lm function, which requires maintaining the row count for the analysis.

The problem I am currently facing is that the results from the procD.lm analysis return very large SS and MS values, and the coefficients suggest a total loss of the geometric shape of the analyzed structure. I constructed the procD.lm function as follows:

TGU.SIM.aov <- procD.lm(TGU.AFA$symm.shape ~ TGU1$LID + TGU1$sexo, Cov = cov_matrix, iter = 9999, RRPP = TRUE, SS.type = "III")

The resulting output is: 

            Df         SS         MS    Rsq      F       Z   Pr(>F)    
TGU1$LID    2 0.0000e+00 0.0000e+00 0.0000  0.000 -8.3013   1.000    
TGU1$sexo   1 5.3796e+10 5.3796e+10 0.0833 25.808  3.9409  1e-04 ***
Residuals 284 5.9200e+11 2.0845e+09 0.9167                          
Total     287 6.4580e+11

Could you kindly help me understand what might be going wrong here?

Thank you very much for your time and assistance!

Best regards,
Federico Fiad

Additionally, I’d appreciate any recommendations for graphical methods to report the results of this model. I also wanted to ask if there are other model validation approaches available within procD.lm, apart from inspecting the residuals plots.

Thanks in advance for your help!

Best regards,
Federico

parts:
Hi Federico,

Great, almost there. First, I provide a better alternative, then I respond to your questions.

Using cov_spatial:
cov.spatial is now defunct, but you can use something like
library(convoSPAT)
#https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/convoSPAT/versions/1.2.7/topics/cov_spatial
cov_matrix <- cov_spatial(dist_matrix, cov.model = "gaussian")
procD.lm(TGU.AFA$symm.shape ~ TGU1$LID + TGU1$sexo, Cov = cov_matrix, iter = 9999, RRPP = TRUE, SS.type = "III")

cov_spatial outputs a spatial covariance matrix and does not require supplied values of the variance or phi. Please be careful and note that cov_spatial requires the supplied dist_matrix to be scaled. Next, I would change the cov.model argument in cov_spatial() to other models and use AIC to see which spatial dependence structure gives the best model fit.

To respond to your concerns:
There is no requirement for SS or MS to be particular values in regression, the magnitude is completely dependent on the data and model. That said, if the high values of SS and MS surprise you, there may be an issue with the units or scaling at some point in your pipeline, I would double check you supplied the right inputs to each function. The values might have blown up because you used PC scores, which scale the data and this might result in unexpected changes, but that is only a wild guess. 

I am not sure what you mean by "the coefficients suggest a total loss of the geometric shape of the analyzed structure". A final note about your pipeline is that it confounds spatial dependence with the covariates in your model (sex and LID). For this reason, people usually interpret variograms of the residuals for learning about model fits. 

Shape data and variograms:
Using PC1 for the variogram is limiting, you should use all the data going into your final model instead. I am not sure if there is a function out there for easily and correctly obtaining a variogram from shape data, but you could always plot this manually. This would entail estimating the semivariance is 0.5*var(pairs), where pairs is the set of all pairwise distances among points a specific distance apart. This can be repeated n(n-1)/2 times across all pairs of n distinct locations, then you can plot semivariance vs distance. Each individual pairwise distance should be the procrustes distance, which is outputted by gpagen(). So, you are set for plotting the variogram for the raw data. 

There might be an easy way of doing the same for model residuals, but I do not know exactly how off the top of my head. More knowledgeable folks on the list can give better advice than I and comment on whether estimating procrustes distances between individuals from the residuals makes sense to begin with. 

Hope that helps!
Bryan

El mar, 1 oct 2024 a las 10:27, Bryan H. Juarez (<bryanh...@gmail.com>) escribió:
Your data might already show spatial dependence in a variogram and you can always plot variability among data points vs distance before generating any matrices.

In addition to the raw data variogram from above, it might also be helpful to use an AIC approach to choose among a set spatial dependence structures by creating variograms from the residuals of alternative models. This is important to take covariates into account. Included among these alternative models you can compare a model with no spatial dependence and this is preferable to only picking one matrix. For example, residuals from models with exponential decay of correlations among sites will have a different pattern than the same but with Gaussian decay of similarities among sites, but both might perform better or similar to a model without spatial dependence (this is data specific).

Cheers,
Bryan

Regarding the distance matrix, I wanted to ask if it is necessary to first perform a variogram analysis to estimate spatial dependence before creating the matrix.

El vie, 27 sept 2024 a las 15:27, Bryan H. Juarez (<bryanh...@gmail.com>) escribió:
Hi Federico, 

I just wanted to add a perspective here regarding your locality data. 

If you have GPS coordinates and can estimate geographical distances among sites, it might be preferable to use the geographic distance matrix as input to the model in the form of a covariance matrix (use the Cov = argument in procD.lm) representing how you think covariation in your shapes is structured among sites. 

If you choose to use this approach, you might find cov.spatial in the geoR library useful, where you can specify if covariance between localities decays with distance following different functions (a Gaussian, exponential, etc.). 

Best,
Bryan
